summary:
On a Mars mission a medical question takes 11 minutes to reach Earth and another 11 minutes for the answer to come back, so no flight surgeon can react in real time and the astronaut becomes the first responder.

Paean is an onboard health console built for that gap, named for the physician to the gods in Homer's Iliad who heals the wounded right on the battlefield. The crew member opens a body map that marks six body systems as Nominal, Watch or Act and clicks any system to see its trends, with every indicator explained in plain language. When a value drifts, Paean opens a standing order that says which countermeasure to start now, how to re-check and when to call Earth, and a 7-sol forecast shows where the value goes with and without that action.

A two-minute daily check-in collects mood, sleep, heart rate and a reaction test and updates the whole console. The Escalate view puts what the crew member sees now beside what Houston sees, which is always minutes old, and tracks the message across the real distance between Earth and Mars. The radiation dose comes from real measurements by NASA's Curiosity rover, including a solar particle event that reached Mars in September 2017.

Crews on long missions can catch problems early and act with confidence before help can answer, and the same approach fits lunar bases, Antarctic stations and remote clinics on Earth.
details:
The Problem

NASA's Human Research Program names five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. A flight surgeon can watch ISS crews in near real time, but that stops working on the way to Mars, where the one-way light time in our mission scenario is 11 min 05 s and the fastest possible answer to any question is more than 22 minutes away. Most health dashboards assume someone on the ground is reading them, whereas Paean assumes the crew member is alone, is not a doctor and has to decide what to do.

Our approach

Paean is a decision-support tool in which every screen answers the questions an astronaut has: what is wrong, why it matters, what to do now and when to call Earth.

1. The body map is a clickable human figure that marks six body systems (cardiovascular, skeletal, neuro-ocular, immune, metabolic and behavioral) by status, with a status rail listing the same systems for anyone who would rather not click the figure. The header shows the mission sol, the environment, the live Earth link delay, the radiation dose against the career limit and a readiness score from 0 to 100.

2. In the system detail view, each of the 15 indicators has a chart of the last 14 sols and a 7-sol forecast that branches into no action and following the countermeasure, along with two short plain-language notes on what it measures and why it matters. Any indicator on Watch or Act opens a standing order with a countermeasure, a self-check and an escalation threshold, and because the flight surgeon pre-authorizes these orders, the crew member knows which actions they can take alone.

3. The daily check-in is a two-minute routine that collects mood, sleep hours, resting heart rate and a 5-tap reaction test by keyboard or mouse, and submitting it updates every chart, the body map and the readiness score and extends the check-in streak.

4. Escalate to Earth places the crew member's current readings beside Houston's picture of them, which lags by the one-way delay, writes the message in the clinical SBAR format (Situation, Background, Assessment, Request), shows the earliest possible reply time and lists what to do in the meantime.

5. The radiation view charts the daily dose for the last 30 sols from real NASA measurements, including a solar particle event, and a second chart projects when career dose reaches the 600 mSv limit, using the lower surface rate after landing. A standing order covers what to do during a solar particle event.

Status uses three tiers everywhere, each with its own shape: Nominal for in range, Watch for out of range or trending wrong, and Act for a crossed threshold. A system takes the worst status of its indicators, and readiness starts at 100 and loses 7 points for each indicator on Watch and 15 for each on Act.

The console can also switch between the transit habitat at 0 g and the surface base at 0.38 g, which changes the radiation dose rate, the hazard description for each system and the fluid shift shown on the body map.
